content: Motofen is a brand-name medication classified as an antiperistaltic anti-diarrheal agent. It contains two active ingredients: 1.0 mg of difenoxin hydrochloride and 0.025 mg of atropine sulfate. Difenoxin is chemically related to opioids, which gives it the potential for misuse. To mitigate this risk, atropine is included in the formulation. Atropine not only discourages misuse due to its unpleasant side effects at higher doses but also contributes to the medication's therapeutic effects by slowing intestinal motility. Despite the low likelihood of misuse, prolonged use of Motofen may lead to physical withdrawal symptoms. It is important to note that Motofen is distinct from Lomotil, as the two medications contain different active ingredients, except for the shared inclusion of atropine. Clinical studies suggest that Motofen is approximately two to four times more effective than Lomotil in managing diarrhea symptoms. The primary FDA-approved indication for Motofen is the treatment of diarrhea. However, physicians have also used it off-label to manage symptoms of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and hyperhidrosis (a condition characterized by excessive sweating). Motofen may cause a range of side effects, including drowsiness, nausea, vomiting, burning or dry eyes, blurred vision, dizziness, dry mouth, epigastric discomfort, and constipation. Some of these side effects, particularly flushing, urinary retention, insomnia, headache, anxiety, hyperthermia, and tachycardia, are specifically associated with atropine, especially when taken in excessive doses or by children. These atropine-related side effects make it undesirable for most patients to take higher-than-recommended doses of the medication. The recommended initial dose of Motofen is two tablets, followed by one tablet after each loose stool. The maximum daily dose should not exceed eight tablets, which corresponds to 8 mg of difenoxin. Although Motofen has been used successfully to treat IBS and hyperhidrosis, there are no official dosing guidelines for these conditions. A lower-strength version of Motofen, containing 0.5 mg of difenoxin per tablet (with the same amount of atropine), was previously available but has since been discontinued. Currently, only the standard 1.0 mg strength tablets are available by prescription. Motofen is manufactured exclusively by Valeant Pharmaceuticals, which acquired the drug from Amarin Pharmaceuticals in 2004. The tablets are pentagonal in shape, with a V debossed on one side and a vertical score line on the other. The number 0500 is debossed across the score line, with 05 on the left and 00 on the right. Motofen is more expensive than other anti-diarrheal medications such as Imodium and Lomotil. It does not have a generic equivalent and is only available by prescription in the United States. Most U.S. insurance companies do not include Motofen in their formularies, resulting in high out-of-pocket costs for patients. The high price of Motofen, combined with the availability of less expensive alternatives, likely explains why it is not approved or sold in other countries. However, these alternatives, such as loperamide and Lomotil, appear to be less effective in managing IBS and hyperhidrosis symptoms. Interestingly, Motofen was only briefly included in the Physicians' Desk Reference (PDR) for the years 2005 and 2006, with minimal information provided beyond its ingredients, appearance, National Drug Code (NDC) number, and packaging details. Despite this, Motofen remains available in the United States and can be found in pharmacies, particularly in larger metropolitan areas. Pharmacists may be unfamiliar with the medication due to its limited use and high cost, often expressing surprise when they discover it in stock.
